Every method takes something for granted about its data: an assumption. When an
assumption is wrong, the model still gives an answer, but the answer can be wrong.
Machine-learning methods are often called assumption-free. They take less for granted
about the shape of a relationship than a linear model does, but they still need data
collected in a way that lets the stations stand for the sea. The five pages in this
section cover three ideas, on the same simulated survey as the rest of the course.

Machine learning frees a model from straight lines and bell curves:

- **linearity and nonlinearity**: a straight line misses the hump of a species'
  preferred temperature, and a random forest finds it without being told its shape;
- **distributional assumptions**: a random forest's errors are lopsided and widen with
  the catch, yet it predicts well; the loss decides what it aims at, the average for
  squared error and the median for absolute error.

It does not free a model from how the data were collected:

- **dependent data**: visits to one site repeat each other, and resampling whole sites
  instead of single stations measures how many fewer independent stations the survey's
  rows are worth;
- **uneven sampling and extrapolation**: cold, shallow winter water that a summer survey
  never met passes a range check on each input; the distance to the nearest surveyed
  station finds it, and a random forest's error grows with that distance.

And a rare answer fools accuracy:

- **class imbalance**: a model can be highly accurate yet miss most of a rare species'
  presences, and rebalancing the training data turns out to move the threshold.

The section picks up threads from earlier ones and passes some on.
[Distributional assumptions](distributional-assumptions.qmd) asks what each loss of
[Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd) aims at.
[Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) kept each site's visits on one
side of the split; [Dependent data](dependent-data.qmd) measures what those visits are
worth, and [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd)
holds out neighbouring sites and whole years.
[Uneven sampling and extrapolation](sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) measures how far a
station lies from the survey as [k-nearest neighbours](../03-supervised-learning/nearest-neighbours.qmd)
finds its neighbours. [Class imbalance](class-imbalance.qmd) builds on the threshold of
[Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) and leaves the
measures that count misses and false alarms apart to
[Classification performance measures](../07-validation/classification-metrics.qmd).

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [spatialsample](https://spatialsample.tidymodels.org/), tidymodels. Blocked, clustered and buffered resampling for data with a location, for when neighbouring sites share conditions too.
- [Common pitfalls and recommended practices](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html), scikit-learn. Independence is assumed silently in almost every default, and this page says where.
